title: The courts
hookLine: Hasidic dynasties such as Ger, Belz, Satmar and Bobov are named for towns
last: GOD'S WILL CAN HIDE INSIDE OUR CHOICES.

lines: A COAT, A BUS, A QUESTION.
cards: A man in a long black coat steps off a bus in Brooklyn, or in Jerusalem, and someone asks him where he's from. He names a town in Europe he may never have visited. A small place, a dot on a map.
He isn't confused about his address. He's telling you which family of Hasidim he belongs to. Hasidic courts often go by neither a founder's name nor an idea, but by a place.

teach.b: The courts. In Yiddish, a hoyf: the court that gathers around a rebbe. First, the names.
Ger comes from Góra Kalwaria, a town near Warsaw. Belz is a town in Galicia. Satmar is the Yiddish name for Satu Mare, in Romania.

Bobov is Bobowa, in southern Poland. And Lubavitch, the name carried by the court of Shneur Zalman's Chabad line, is a small town too. Each court took its name from the place where its rebbe lived and Hasidim came to him.
Second, the dynasty. Earlier in this block you met the rebbe as guide for his followers.
When a rebbe dies, a court usually looks for the next one in his family: a son, a son-in-law, a grandson. So the name, the melodies and the customs pass down like an heirloom.
Sometimes two heirs each draw followers, and one court becomes two. Third, the move. The Jewish life of these towns was destroyed in the Holocaust.

Survivors carried the courts to new homes, in places like Brooklyn, Jerusalem and Bnei Brak. The town is gone from their daily life, but its name still stands over the door. Fourth, what it means for a Hasid.
To say I'm a Belzer, or a Bobover, is to say: this is my rebbe, these are my tunes, this is how my family prays and dresses and marks the festivals.
Each court has its own feel. None speaks for all Hasidim, and Hasidim don't all agree about each other.
It's the old Hebrew sense of a court, a courtyard, a gathering place: "a day in thy courts is better than a thousand."

how: Hasidim belong to a particular court and its rebbe, often for generations; they pray in that court's synagogues, sing its melodies and keep its customs, and gather at the rebbe's table on Shabbat and festivals.

o: Hasidic communities around a rebbe, named for towns
the rabbinic law courts that settle Jewish disputes
the open courtyards of the Temple in Jerusalem

games.q: named for towns — tap the pairs.

s: a court usually looks for its next rebbe in the family
a son, a son-in-law, a grandson: the line passes like an heirloom.
a Hasid who says "I'm a Belzer" was born in Belz

games.q: you meet a man in Jerusalem who says he's a Bobover. what is he telling you?
o: he follows the Bobov rebbe and its customs.
he works for a company called Bobov.
games.why: the court took its name from the town where it began. the name traveled with the Hasidim to their new homes.

practice: Say one name from today quietly a few times: Ger, Belz, Satmar, Bobov or Lubavitch.

Then think of a place your own family carries in its name or its stories, a town, a street, a country someone left, and what you still do because of it: a food, a word, a habit. Sit with the two places side by side.

wordCard.voice: The courts. The Hasidic communities gathered around a rebbe, usually passed down within his family, and named for the European towns where they began. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a court or courtyard, as in the Psalm's "thy courts". Yiddish speakers call a rebbe's court a hoyf.

carryVoice: Your line: named for towns. A name can carry a whole way of life across an ocean. Back tomorrow, same hill.
